title: 簗氏予算カット発言 収束見通せず
body:
高市首相が８日の代表質問で簗農相の続投を表明したのは、地元自治体の道路予算を巡る発言を問題視しつつも予算減額の働きかけを否定した国土交通省の調査結果などを考慮したからだ。政府・与党は事態の収束を図りたい考えだが、国会審議への影響は避けられない状況で、幕引きは見通せない。（谷口京子）【表】大幅に減っている…「大幅にカットした」と言われた２市町への道路整備関連の国交付金
「私の不徳によるもので不適切だったと自覚している」。簗氏はこの日、衆参両院の代表質問で答弁に立ち、低姿勢で釈明を重ねた。首相も簗氏を厳しく注意したと説明した上で、引き続き職務に当たらせる考えを強調した。
簗氏はすでに発言を撤回して謝罪し、国交省は道路予算の減額への働きかけは「なかったとみられる」との調査結果を発表した。首相周辺は「本人や政府が答えられることは全て答えた」とし、これ以上の説明は難しいとの認識を示す。
内閣改造直後に閣僚を交代させれば、首相の任命責任が問われるのは必至となる。今年３月には松本洋平文部科学相（当時）が女性問題で追及されたが、続投で乗り切り、政権発足後、不祥事などで交代した閣僚はいない。
首相が簗氏を買っていることも擁護姿勢につながっているとみられる。首相は２月の衆院選の応援演説で簗氏を「私の大事なやなちゃん」と親しみを込めて紹介した。簗氏は自民党派閥の政治資金問題で収支報告書に１７４６万円の不記載があったが、入閣させた。
一方、野党は簗氏の資質にも矛先を向け、追及を続ける構えだ。選挙での支援と予算を絡めた発言の性質に批判が集中している。
立憲民主党の田名部幹事長は８日の参院代表質問で、「予算を政治的な報復や見返りに用いようとする姿勢は到底許されない。撤回、謝罪だけで済むとお考えか」と迫った。共産党の田村委員長は記者会見で「有権者を恫喝（どうかつ）しているに等しい」と指弾した。
国会審議への影響も不可避の情勢となっている。立民の斎藤嘉隆国会対策委員長は自民の磯崎仁彦参院国対委員長と国会内で会談し、参院農林水産委員会で簗氏の所信聴取に応じないと伝えた。斎藤氏は記者団に「早期に大臣の職を退かれることを強く求めたい」と語った。
簗氏を巡っては、８日発売の週刊文春が、過去の衆院選で支持者をシャトルバスで無料送迎したことが公職選挙法に違反する疑いがあると新たに報じた。自民内では「世論の動向次第では、続投を貫き通せるかわからない」（閣僚経験者）との声も出ている。

title: 露でペスト疑い 接触者に異常なし
body:
ロシアの公衆衛生当局は８日、東シベリア・イルクーツクのペスト対策研究所の女性職員が死亡してペスト感染が懸念された事案に関し、接触者全員に「健康上の異常は確認されなかった」と発表した。予防措置を完了したとしており、地元住民に感染が拡大するリスクはないと判断した模様だ。【写真】ロシアのプーチン大統領
発表は「約５０００件の検査から、危険な病原菌は検出されなかった」と説明した。当初、死亡した職員と接触した可能性のある約２００人が隔離されたとの情報もあったが、検査対象となった接触者の人数や防疫措置の具体的な内容は明らかにされていない。
発表では、職員が死亡した事実や死因についての言及もなかった。４日の発表では、「原因不明の肺炎」と診断された職員の検体からは「業務に関連する微生物は検出されなかった」として、ペスト感染を改めて否定していた。
危険な感染症の拡大が懸念される中、米国はさらなる情報提供を行うようロシアに求めていた。ロシア当局は７日、今回の事案に関する情報を世界保健機関（ＷＨＯ）に報告したと明らかにしていた。
ただ、複数の独立系メディアによると、当初「ペストの疑いのある患者が死亡した」などと伝えたテレビや新聞の報道は、ＳＮＳやホームページから次々と削除されている。ウクライナに対する侵略の長期化を背景にプーチン政権は人心の動揺を警戒し、報道統制を敷いている可能性がある。

title: 米国防総省 銃殺刑を生配信へ
body: 【AFP＝時事】米国防総省当局者は8日、2009年に南部テキサス州のフォートフッド陸軍基地で銃を乱射して13人を殺害し、殺人罪などで死刑判決を受けた元軍医ニダル・ハサン死刑囚の銃殺刑を生配信すると明らかにした。ピート・ヘグセス国防長官はこれに先立ち、同死刑囚を「公開」処刑すると述べていた。【写真】死刑生き延びた殺人犯、意識戻り会話可能に 米テネシー州国防総省当局者は匿名を条件にAFPの取材に応じ、ハサン死刑囚の銃殺刑について「生配信される。詳細は追って発表する」と述べた。ヘグセス氏は8日、X（旧ツイッター）の国防総省公式アカウントに投稿された動画で、ハサン死刑囚について「当然のことながら、兵士から成る銃殺隊によって処刑される。公開で執行する」と述べていた。ヘグセス氏は米空母エーブラハム・リンカーンの艦上で、右派インフルエンサーのジャック・ポソビエック氏に対し、「こうした行為には重大な結果が伴うことを、人々は理解する必要がある」と語った。ヘグセス氏は、米軍による銃殺刑の執行は第2次世界大戦以来になると指摘した。1945年に脱走・敵前逃亡の罪で銃殺刑に処されたエディ・スロビク死刑囚の事例に言及したものだ。ヘグセス氏は「私は第2次世界大戦時の精神が嫌いではない。すなわち勝利を第一に考え、敵が攻撃してきた時は、一歩も引かずに立ち向かわなければならないと理解する心構えだ」と述べた。別の動画では、ポソビエック氏がヘグセス氏に対し、ハサン死刑囚の最後の願いは何だったかを尋ねた。ヘグセス氏は「どうでもいい。12月3日に会おう」と答えた。12月3日はハサン死刑囚の死刑執行予定日だ。米軍が最後に死刑を執行したのは1961年で、ジョン・ベネット死刑囚がレイプと殺人未遂の罪で絞首刑に処された。【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: ブックオフ 約643万件情報流出か
body: ブックオフグループホールディングスは10月9日、子会社の会員管理システムが第三者による不正アクセスを受け、会員情報最大約643万件が外部に流出したと発表した。流出の詳細（適時開示より）流出した可能性があるのは、氏名、生年月日、性別、メールアドレス、電話番号、郵便番号・住所、パスワードのハッシュ値、ポイントカード番号、会員番号。643万件は会員番号の件数で、実際の人数ではないとしている。クレジットカード情報などの決済情報は同システムで保有していないため含まれない。不正アクセスは10月6日に確認。調査した結果、同システムで管理している会員情報が外部から取得されたことが分かった。攻撃元からの通信を遮断し、脆弱性を是正した上で、対象システムへの外部からのアクセスを遮断して監視を続けている。9日時点で、流出した情報が外部に公開された事実や第三者に悪用された事実、会員情報の書き換えは確認していない。同社は全システムを対象に緊急総点検を実施しており、ネットワークとアプリケーションの両面から追加の安全対策と恒久的な再発防止策を進めるという。対象者には調査結果を踏まえて順次個別に連絡する。同社グループや関係先を装ったメール、SMS、電話が送られる可能性があるとして注意を呼びかけている。対象者の人数と漏えいした可能性がある情報は引き続き精査しており、詳細が分かり次第、続報で知らせる。

title: タイヤ交換中に破裂 作業員が死亡
body: 北海道苫小牧市の運送会社でトラックのタイヤが破裂する事故があり、50代後半の男性従業員が死亡しました。事故があったのは苫小牧市一本松町の運送会社の敷地内です。10月8日午後4時10分ごろ、「大型車両のタイヤがバーストした。男性が負傷している」と消防から警察に通報がありました。この事故で、従業員の50代後半の男性1人が病院に搬送されましたが、死亡が確認されました。警察によりますと、当時、男性はトラックのタイヤ交換作業のため、1人でタイヤを運んでいました。別の従業員が「バンッ」という破裂音を聞いて駆け付けたところ、破裂したタイヤの近くに男性が倒れていたということです。別の従業員にケガはありません。警察は当時の状況やタイヤが破裂した原因を調べています。

title: 中間選挙前に攻撃しない 米大統領
body: [ワシントン ８日 ロイター] - トランプ米大統領は８日、１１月の米中間選挙前にイランへの攻撃は‌実施しないと表明した。戦争の終結に向⁠け、両国は「建設的な」協議を行っているとした。トランプ氏は自身の交流サイト（ＳＮＳ）「トゥルース・​ソーシャル」への投稿で、「イランと建設的な協議を行っている。われわれは１１月３日‌に米国で行われる中間選挙まで、いかなる時点においてもイランを攻撃することはない」‌と述べた。今年２月に米国とイ‌スラエルによるイラン攻撃で始まっ​た戦争は、トランプ氏の国内支持率を押し下げる要因‌となっている。１１月の選挙で上下両院の多数派を維持しようとする共和党‌にとっても重い足かせ​となっている。ロイター／イプソスが最近実施した‌世論調査によると、米国民の約６０％がトランプ氏のイラン対応を⁠支持しないと回答した。共和党支持者でも４人に１人が不支持だった。有権者が最大の関心事に生活費を挙げる中、紛争⁠はガソリン価格を大きく押し上げて​いる。イランと米国‌はここ数週間、戦争の終結と、世界のエネルギー輸送の要衝であるホルムズ海峡の再開に向けた提案を交わ⁠してきた。トランプ氏はイラン側の最新⁠の提案を拒否した。イランのエスラミ原子力庁長官は、米国が⁠イランに対しウラン濃縮能力の「意味のある」削減を求めたこ‌とを受け、⁠イランはウラン濃縮活動を放棄せず、保有​するウランを引き渡すこともないと述べた。国営メディアが８日報じた。

title: ロシア ICC所長らの引き渡し要求
body: ロシア最高検察庁は8日、ロシアで有罪判決が出ている国際刑事裁判所（ICC）の赤根智子所長らの身柄を引き渡すよう、ICCの本部があるオランダを含む複数の国に要請したと発表した。ICCは2023年にウクライナ侵攻をめぐり、ロシアのプーチン大統領らへの逮捕状を発付しており、ロシアは対抗措置を強めてきた。近年は米国のトランプ政権もICCへの圧力を強めている。【写真】インタビューに答えるICCの赤根智子所長最高検察庁は声明で、赤根氏やカーン元主任検察官、ホフマンスキー元所長らの拘束と引き渡しを要求。理由として「法的根拠がないにもかかわらず、明らかに違法な逮捕状の発行を命じた」などと主張している。ただ、オランダはイェッテン首相が「ICCに手を出すな」と訴えるなど、ICCを擁護する立場を鮮明にしている。実際に引き渡しに応じる可能性は低いとみられる。ICCは23年3月、ウクライナ侵攻をめぐる戦争犯罪容疑などでプーチン氏に逮捕状を出した。ロシアはこれに強く反発。モスクワの裁判所が25年12月、プーチン氏らに違法に逮捕状を出したなどとして、赤根氏やカーン氏らに欠席裁判で3年半～15年の拘禁刑を言い渡していた。ICCをめぐっては、米国も近年、対立姿勢を強めている。トランプ政権は今年8月に赤根氏への制裁を発表。トランプ大統領はICCを「邪悪な集団」と批判し、加盟国に脱退を呼びかけるなど、圧力を強めている。

title: 韓国とウクライナ 対立深まる背景
body:
韓国とウクライナの外交的な対立が深まっている。発端はロシアに派兵された北朝鮮軍の捕虜をめぐる問題だが、今度は韓国からロシアへの石油製品輸出疑惑に飛び火した。
ウクライナのゼレンスキー大統領は9月23日、国連総会での演説で、北朝鮮軍捕虜2人を韓国に移送したと発言した。これに韓国の李在明大統領が、非公開の合意を破ったとして反発。ウクライナ側は合意の存在を否定し、両国間で異例の応酬が繰り広げられた。
「事実上、韓国からの輸入は、ロシアが自国の精製能力を失った影響を相殺するのを助けた」出典：金賢　2026/10/7(水)
韓国大統領府は７日、ロシアが韓国の港から石油製品を輸入‌したとするウクライナの報道を否定し、⁠その非難は不適切だと述べた出典：ロイター　2026/10/8(木)
捕虜の韓国送還の事実を公開した背景には、韓国からパトリオット防空ミサイルシステムの支援を受けられなかったことへの不満出典：中央日報日本語版　2026/9/29(火)
「朝鮮半島での戦争勃発を願うウクライナに深刻な遺憾を表する」出典：金賢　2026/10/5(月)
李在明大統領はその後、ウクライナが「朝鮮半島での戦争勃発を願っている」と受け取れる発言まで行い、謝罪を要求した。
そして10月6日、ウクライナ大統領府のブラシウク顧問が、韓国の港からロシアに石油製品約17万6000トンが輸送され、ロシアの燃料不足を緩和したと批判。翌7日、韓国大統領府は事実関係の確認が不十分だとして反論した。
両国の対立の背景には、北朝鮮に対する根本的な認識の違いがある。
韓国にとって北朝鮮は、軍事的な脅威であると同時に、衝突を避けながら関係を管理しなければならない隣国だ。捕虜の受け入れも、金正恩政権を刺激しかねない厄介な問題なのである。
一方、ウクライナにとって北朝鮮は、自国の兵士を殺傷するために軍隊と兵器を送り込んできた敵国だ。しかも、韓国はウクライナが求める直接的な軍事支援に応じていない。ウクライナ側に不満が蓄積していても不思議ではない。
皮肉なのは、ロシアと北朝鮮の軍事協力によって安全保障上の脅威に直面する両国が、互いへの不信を強めていることだ。結果として、この対立が利益をもたらす相手は、ほかならぬロシアと北朝鮮ではないだろうか。

title: 蛇口の水恐怖 ネパールでトラウマ
body:
【カトマンズ共同】8月にネパールを襲った大規模な土石流被害の支援に当たる国連児童基金（ユニセフ）のジェームズ・エルダー広報官は8日、首都カトマンズで共同通信の取材に応じ「被災してトラウマ（心的外傷）を抱えた子どもの心理的サポートが課題だ」と語った。蛇口から出る水を見て土石流を連想し、恐怖を感じる子どももいるという。【写真】大規模な洪水に襲われ、泥に覆われた家屋＝8月、ネパール中部
ユニセフによると、被災した子どもは約3万2千人に上る。学校23校が損壊したため、ユニセフは約50カ所の仮設学習センターを設け、1400人以上の子どもの学習環境を整えた。カウンセラーが相談に乗る態勢を取っている。土石流は8月26日、ネパールと中国の国境付近で発生し、ネパールの川沿いにある建物の多くを直撃した。ユニセフはテントや毛布、おむつなどの物資を送り届け、被災した120世帯を対象に世帯当たり1万5千ルピー（約1万5300円）の現金を給付して支援した。エルダー氏は子どもの学費を例に挙げ、1年から1年半は現金給付を続けるべきだとの意向を示した。

title: プルデンシャル 背景に独特の文化
body:
プルデンシャル生命保険の金銭詐取問題を巡る第三者委員会の調査報告書は、行き過ぎた成果主義や経営陣の監督不足を厳しく指弾した。今後、報酬体系の見直しや顧客対応の透明化など抜本改革に取り組む構えだが、被害補償や金融庁の行政処分を控える中、組織の立て直しは容易でない。（川崎大輝、松本健太朗）【図】社員が不正を始めた時点の年齢・報酬・在籍年数
「局所的な対応にとどまっていた部分は、重く受け止めている。カルチャー変革まで踏み込んだ抜本的な改革を進めていく必要がある」。得丸博充社長は８日の記者会見で、苦渋の表情を見せた。
１６０ページ超に及ぶ調査報告書は、１９９２～２０２５年の３０年以上にわたり不正を見逃してきた背景に、同社独特の営業文化があったことを浮き彫りにした。
その一つが「ライフプランナー（ＬＰ）」と呼ばれる営業社員で、顧客一人ひとりの人生設計に寄り添い、保険の提案から契約後の相談まで幅広く対応する。徹底した成果主義が課され、新規契約を多く獲得したＬＰほど高額な報酬を得られる。優秀な成績をあげると毎年、ハワイや沖縄などに招待され、「社長杯」として表彰されるなど、競争意識を高める「独自のカルチャー」が形成されていった。
こうした営業文化は、顧客との関係が特定の社員に集中する「個人化」と、営業活動の実態が同僚・上司から見えなくなる「密室化」を招いた。第三者委によると、ある営業社員は顧客に対し、「資金を預ければ、一定期間かけて元本を上回る金額を返還する」などと投資を持ちかけ、複数回にわたって金銭を不正に受け取った。両者の関係は社員の退職後も続き、顧客が返済を求めても「運用状況が芳しくない」と説明し、受け取った金額の一部しか返さなかったという。
管理職となる営業所長や支社長の報酬は、配下ＬＰの業績で大部分が決まる仕組みとなり、第三者委は報告書で、こうした営業モデルに不正のリスクが構造的に内在していたと認定した。報告書によると、２５年度は年間報酬が３０００万円超が約４００人、中には３億円を超える社員もいた。だが、不正が大きいとされる社員に限れば、年間報酬８００万円未満が５５％を占める。優秀な業績を上げられずに収入が不足し、不正に手を染めていった実態も浮き彫りになった。

title: プルデンシャル 不正巡り64人解雇
body: プルデンシャル生命保険は8日、営業社員らが顧客から金銭をだまし取るなどしていた問題を巡り、外部の弁護士らで作る特別調査委員会の報告書を公表した。【写真まとめ】謝罪するプルデンシャル生命保険の社長の表情報告書を受け、得丸博充社長ら役員3人が3カ月間、報酬を30％自主返納するとした。また、詐取問題に関与した営業社員（退職者含む）157人のうち、64人を懲戒解雇・諭旨解雇▽68人を業務停止▽25人を訓戒などの処分――にしたと発表した。午後3時から、得丸社長が東京都内で記者会見を開き、報告書の内容や再発防止策を説明する。【横見知佳】

title: 米スタバ メキシコ料理買収を検討
body: [８日 ロイター] - 米コーヒーチェーン大手スターバックス（スタバ）は８日、メキシコ料理チェーンのチポトレ・メキシカン・グリルの買収を模索しているとの報道についてコメントを控え、ブ‌ライアン・ニコル最高経営責任者（ＣＥＯ）の下での経営立て直しに「全力で集中している」と表明し⁠た。英紙フィナンシャル・タイムズ（ＦＴ）はこれに先立ち、関係者の話として、スタバがここ数カ月、チポトレ買収の可能性についてアドバイザーと協議を進めてきたと報じた。ニコル氏は２０２４年にスタバのトップに就任するまで、​約６年間チポトレを率いていた。買収が実現すれば、米外食業界を代表する２ブランドの統合となり、ニコル氏がチポトレに再び関与することになる。スタバの広報担当者は報道を受け、うわさや‌臆測にはコメントしないと述べた。ニコル氏の下で２年間にわたり進めている経営立て直しに引き続き注力しており、力強い勢いを維持し、長期的な成長の可能性に自信を持っているとした。チポトレはロイターのコメン‌ト要請に応じなかった。時価総額が約１０７０億ドルのスタバ‌の株価は８日、下げ幅を縮小し、ほぼ横ばいで取引を終えた。一方、チポトレ株は６％上​昇し、時価総額は約４１０億ドルとなった。ニコル氏はチポトレ在籍中、食品安全問題を巡る危機の余波を乗り切り、デジタル事業を拡大した手腕‌を評価された。こうした取り組みは、数年にわたる力強い売上高の伸びにつながった。ＲＢＣキャピタル・マーケッツのアナリスト、ローガン・ライヒ氏は「チポトレに‌とっては、主にニコル氏が同ブランドに戻る​という点から、好意的に受け止められると考える」と述べた。その上で、外食企業が成長を促‌すために他のブランドを買収することに投資家は懐疑的だと指摘。スタバによるチポトレ買収の戦略的な合理性は不明確だと語った。＜買収に⁠多額の費用負担も＞アナリストらは、スタバがなお経営立て直しに多額の投資を続けていることから、買収には大きな費用負担が伴う可能性が高いと指摘した。イートロのグローバル市場ストラテジスト、ラレ・アコナー氏は「買収には多額の借り入れや新株発行が必要になる⁠可能性がある。財務面で説得力のある根拠がなければ、投資家は本業への集中を​そぐ高くつく買収と受け止めるかも‌しれない」と述べた。アネックス・ウェルス・マネジメントのチーフ経済ストラテジスト、ブライアン・ジェイコブセン氏も「スタバは改革の途上にあり、投資家が期待しているであろう利益率の改善もまだ示していないことを考えると、買収のタイ⁠ミングにはやや違和感がある。第一印象では、改革を加速するというより、奇策に走って道を誤るよう⁠に見える」と述べた。一方、チポトレは消費者が裁量的な支出を控える中、客足の鈍化に直面している。食品価格や人件費の上昇も外食業界全⁠体の利益率を圧迫している。同社の株価はニコル氏の退任以降、ほぼ半値となった。ただ、一部のアナリストは、買収が実現すればチポトレの海外‌展開が加速す⁠る可能性があると指摘する。ノースコースト・リサーチのアナリスト、ジム・サンダーソン氏は「この​買収の可能性について評価しているのは、ニコルＣＥＯがスタバの欧州でのライセンス提携を活用し、チポトレをより積極的に展開する機会を得られることだ」と述べた。

title: アサヒGHD社長 カルテル認識ない
body: ビールなどの出荷価格を調整する「カルテル」を結んだ疑いがあるとして、公正取引委員会は大手ビールメーカー4社に強制調査に入りました。取材で浮かび上がったのは、担当者らによる“非公式会合”の存在でした。【写真で見る】調整は“非公式会合”「一木会」で…値段は“ほぼ横並び”■消費者に余分な負担の可能性…ビール大手4社にカルテル疑い東京・新橋駅前で聞かれた憤りの声。「自由に競争しないで、僕らが払うお金が高くなっているなら、それはフェアじゃない」「裏は絶対あっちゃいけない」「アサヒビール」「キリンビール」「サントリー」「サッポロビール」のビール大手4社が出荷する際の価格を調整する「カルテル」を結んだ疑いがあるとして、公正取引委員会が独占禁止法違反の疑いで4社に強制調査に入りました。ビールはメーカーから「卸業者」へ卸された後、飲食店やスーパー等の「小売業者」で販売され、消費者が購入します。メーカー4社は卸業者向けに出荷する際の価格を不正に調整した疑いがあり、消費者が余分な負担を強いられた可能性があるのです。その調整が行われていたのは、非公式の集まり。東京・銀座に4社が加盟する業界団体「ビール酒造組合」の事務所があります。ここで主に、毎月第1木曜日に「一木会」と呼ばれる会合が開かれていました。この会合前後に4社の営業課長らが非公式に集まり、値上げ幅の具体的な目標を定めるなどしていたとみられています。■調査すると…各社ほぼ同じ価格本来、各企業がそれぞれ決めるべき商品の価格。コンビニ3社の価格を見ると、サントリーは他のメーカーと比べ4〜11円の差がありますが、各社ほぼ横並びの状況です。【コンビニ各社値段比較（350ml缶・新橋駅周辺）】▼A社アサヒビール:227円キリンビール:227円サッポロビール:227円サントリー:223円▼B社アサヒビール:226円キリンビール:226円サッポロビール:226円サントリー:215円▼C社アサヒビール:227円キリンビール:227円サッポロビール:227円サントリー:223円

title: 進む脱炭素 中国依存拡大のリスク
body:
気候変動対策として再生可能エネルギーの普及が進んでいます。他方で、国際社会は脱炭素を進めるほど中国への依存が強まるという矛盾に直面しています。
太陽光パネルや蓄電池、風力タービンといった再エネ機器の製造、さらには不可欠な重要鉱物の精錬工程において、中国企業は8割を超える世界シェアを握り圧倒的な支配力を誇ります。
かつて中東の特定国に原油を頼ってきた「石油の時代」の地政学的脆弱性が、脱炭素時代においては中国一国へ集中的に構造変化を起こしている点が大きなリスクとなっています。
再生エネ発電施設の中国の導入容量は230GWで世界の半分に迫る（中略）脱炭素に関する技術や製品で中国のシェアは圧倒的出典：Sutainable Brands　2024/7/1(月)
中国の脱炭素政策は(中略)フェーズ1から、システム全体の効率化と安定運用を重視するフェーズ2＝「脱炭素2.0」へ出典：Lab research　2026/8/5(水)
日本は脱炭素をめぐる技術や製品では中国依存が進んでおり、サプライチェーン上の脆弱性が指摘されている。出典：東洋経済オンライン　2023/11/14(火)
中国とEUは（中略）組む可能性があります。ヨーロッパ、アメリカ、中国を中心とした21世紀の主導権争いは、今後も続出典：東洋経済オンライン　2022/2/16(水)
政策的に問われているのは、気候変動対策と経済安全保障の完全な両立です。安価な中国製機器に頼り切る安易な脱炭素は、有事の際にエネルギー供給の命ノ節を握られる危険を孕みます。
求められるのは、日米欧を中心とした「脱・中国依存」のサプライチェーン再構築です。国内投資を通じた製造基盤の回帰や次世代技術（ペロブスカイト太陽電池など）の実用化、鉱物資源の友好国間調達ネットワークの確立を加速させなければなりません。
再エネの真の価値は、エネルギー自給による国家の自立にあります。中国主導の価格競争に呑み込まれることなく、自前のインフラと技術を護り抜く「したたかな脱炭素戦略」こそが、今日本を含めた各国に必要とされています。

title: Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire breaks silence to BBC
summary: Vitalii Zhykovych gives his own account of the attempted assassination of Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev.
body:
Vitalii Zhykovych appeared in open court during the summer and has spoken to the BBC from prison
A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was ordered by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time.
Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle".
Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent".
A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head.
But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her.
He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut.
Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych.
Ukrainian agent accused of murdering Monaco bomb suspect changes story
For a long time, Zhykovych himself stayed silent.
Now, responding to questions from the BBC, he alleges that Reut - who he refers to as "The Boss" - had "proposed the operation" in Monaco against Vadym Yermolayev.
He understood it was an official mission.
"As Reut informed me, this operation […] had been authorised and approved by Reut's superiors, who served in the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence [HUR]," he says.
Distancing himself from the explosion itself, he alleges that Reut asked to use Berezovska for the bombing and when Zhykovych refused – he says she was not fully trained – Reut agreed to send her for reconnaissance instead.
Vladyslav Reut initially confessed but then changed his testimony
Reut then communicated directly with Bereszovska without including him, according to Zhykovych, who alleges that Reut also provided her with the explosives.
The BBC asked HUR to comment on the latest claims. The agency has previously said that it is "committed to a full investigation" and providing "comprehensive support" to law enforcement bodies.
The SBU has described Zhykovych in a statement only as a "former law enforcement officer".
Two screengrabs from a surveillance video captured Anastasia Berezovska just before and during the explosion
Yermolayev was attacked in Monaco as he and his family were returning from an evening meal on the seafront. A surveillance video shows Berezovska walking slightly in front of the group, then leaving the device in a bag on their doorstep.
It detonates just as they get close, apparently shocking even Berezovska with its force.
Yermolayev later said he believed that serving HUR officers, "individuals close to the agency's current and former leadership", were linked to the attack.
He called for "the truth, protection, and justice".
Berezovska was quickly identified as the suspected bomber and on 2 July her image, taken from CCTV footage, was circulated by Interpol.
She had already fled, first driving through Italy and Germany, then taking a bus from Frankfurt to Ukraine.
Before she could be caught and questioned though, she was driven to the woods by Reut and Zhykovych and killed. Each blames the other for her shooting.
The shocking case has prompted intense speculation, including over who may have wanted Yermolayev dead and why, and whether this could have been a state-ordered assassination attempt, a rogue operation or some kind of criminal score-settling.
After the Monaco blast, police released an image of Berezovska caught on CCTV
The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories.
They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine.
Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine.
Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case.
Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us.
He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea.
"In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison.
Zhykovych (C) spoke publicly for the first time at a recent custody hearing in Kyiv
Yermolayev has repeatedly denied any remaining business interests linked to Russia.
But might this story be even murkier?
At his most recent custody hearing in Kyiv, surrounded by heavily armed guards, Zhykovych spoke publicly for the first time since his arrest. The BBC were the only media present.
At one point Zhykovych said Reut had in fact told him the attack in Monaco was not "authorised".
"Someone had ordered this target from the civilian side," Zhykovych said, without explaining.
Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries
The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court.
Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets.
When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason.
As the investigation continues – into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own.
The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son.
Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" – meaning Russia.
He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation".
Berezovska's husband has told the BBC that the allegation was "nonsense". He believes she was dragged, unwittingly, into the whole affair.
Zhykovych says Berezovska called him the day after the Monaco attack, and when he asked why she had done it, she said Reut had promised her a huge fee. "$50,000 doesn't just lie on the streets," she supposedly explained.
Residents in her village have told us that Berezovska was saving to buy a flat. But when she travelled to Ukraine to collect the money, she was lured into the woods and shot.
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko and Volodymyr Lozhko.

title: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
summary: The US Defence Secretary says the execution will be public, but a legal expert says the "unprecedented" decision is on "uncertain legal terrain".
body:
The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.
A Defense Department official told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed.
It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The decision to livestream it is "unprecedented in the modern era" and "on uncertain legal terrain," said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."
An undated handout image of Hasan that was released by authorities in 2012
The Pentagon had announced earlier this week that it would execute Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Hegseth said in an interview with conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be".
Asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to President Donald Trump Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said on Monday that the defence secretary had made the recommendation and Trump approved it.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on whether Trump supports a livestreamed public execution.
The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted in court that he was the gunman in the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The shooting on 5 November 2009 took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
At court Hasan apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
Fort Hood attacker to be executed by firing squad - a first for US military since World War Two
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law. It also requires appellate review, where a higher court inspects the decision, and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The appellate process for Hasan is not over, Mills said, and he is likely to seek review of his conviction and sentence in federal court, which would likely stay the execution.
As such, Mills said that he would be surprised if the execution happened.
"Seeking to make it livestreamed, a firing squad execution, is little more than attention-seeking by the Trump administration and is unlikely to occur, much less deliver any semblance of justice," he added.
Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School told the BBC it was a "really unfortunate decision". "To livestream an execution is just so out of the Middle Ages. In a way, we are so past that as a society, at least I thought so until today," he added.
Fiddel said Hasan could pursue legal action that could trigger a lengthy legal process.
"If he does exercise the right, the legal proceedings would last years," Fidell said. "They'd last far longer than President Trump's term in the White House," he added.
Public execution is 'out of the Middle Ages', says Yale professor
Certain states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many states require journalists to be present, and the person due to be executed can invite people. Others also allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses.
But "there hasn't ever been a livestreamed execution," says Deborah Denno, a law professor at Fordham University, who has studied US execution methods.
A livestreamed execution would "force a level of transparency that we have probably never seen before in this country", she says.
"More than half of the country wants the death penalty - even though that's on the decline - an argument could be made that 'if you want the death penalty, then we are going to show you how it's conducted in this country'. And people would have to realise exactly what's happening in a way that many people ignore."
Denno says there are important considerations for a livestream such as whether it would be age-redistricted and whether it would contravene the policies of the online platform that hosts the viewing.
It is unclear where the livestream will be available. Most major social media platforms have rules that prohibit or restrict livestreaming explicit content.
While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two countries carried them out publicly.
Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025, and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International.
The countries with the highest number of executions last year were China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the US, in that order, Amnesty International data shows.
While Trump has never publicly advocated for a public execution, he has long supported the death penalty. In 1989, for example, he took out large ads in The New York Times calling for the execution of the Central Park Five - who had been convicted of rape and assault charges but were later exonerated.
Trump has previously condemned public executions in Iran, and has cited the Iranian government's potential killing of protesters as a possible justification for military intervention before attacking the country earlier this year.
The US government had not executed anyone for 17 years until the final year of Trump's first term as president, when the government conducted a flurry of 13 executions.
Upon returning to office last January, Trump swiftly overturned predecessor Joe Biden's moratorium on federal executions and signed an executive order aimed at "restoring" the death penalty and "protecting public safety".
The last military execution in the country took place in 1961, when a US Army private was hanged after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. The execution was authorised by then-President Dwight D Eisenhower and took place despite the victim's family asking his successor, John F Kennedy, for clemency.
The last military execution by firing squad took place in January 1945, when a young US Army deserter, Eddie Slovik, was shot during the final months of the World War Two.

title: Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
summary: Ukraine accused Russia of targeting two crowded vehicles in the front line city of Kramatorsk to kill as many civilians as possible.
body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv's allies needed to take "concrete action"
At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.
Authorities said three people were also killed in the village of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community.
Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Moscow is trying to seize as part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said: "This strike will not go without our response."
In a post on Telegram, he said: "Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this. React harshly - exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have caused."
Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across Ukraine and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.
According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.
In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who together with Zelensky visited the site of the Russian strike in Pryluky, said the attack showed Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".
He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict".
After the deadly attack on Kramatorsk, Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the eastern front line region to move to safer parts of Ukraine.
Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.
Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched by Putin in 2022 - a claim rejected by Ukraine and its allies as baseless.
Donbas is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.
For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.
Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall.  In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.
Kramatorsk city council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it said.
Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 22 in block of flats
Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas
Russia has in recent weeks been launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing virtually non-stop.
On Thursday, Kyiv police said four people were killed and two injured in the latest Russian attack on the city.
The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into underground shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport.
Moscow's strikes on Ukraine's key infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts.
Kyiv's metro network - which millions of residents rely on - on Thursday briefly halted all its train traffic due to a voltage drop from "external power centres". Trains later started moving again - but at greater intervals, local officials said.
Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".
Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.
Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have.
Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little  chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.
On Thursday, Russian state-run media reported that a number of websites in the country were inaccessible following a Ukrainian drone attack on a data centre of Yandex - Russia's largest search engine.

title: Christa Pike now walking after failed US execution, lawyer tells BBC
summary: A lawyer says the murderer of Colleen Slemmer is moving around her hospital room after surviving two lethal injections.
body:
Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's "shock" recovery in hospital
Christa Pike is "up and walking" though mentally "foggy" while in hospital after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her legal team says.
Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. Experts described it as unprecedented.
Speaking late on Wednesday to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, lawyer Stephen Ferrell said he had not spoken to Pike directly but had learned her arms were swollen and barely functioning as she took her first steps around her hospital room.
A court has ordered state officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.
That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
The Pike case is now in uncharted territory, as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
The failed execution was branded a "mess" by the mother of Slemmer, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death.
Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's gruesome murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
How did Christa Pike survive two lethal injections?
What happens next in the Pike case?
In their previous updates on Pike's condition after the attempted execution, her team had said she was awake and speaking, and experiencing anger and confusion. She was said at that stage to be handcuffed to her bed.
Her lawyer Randy Spivey said after Wednesday's court hearing: "She cannot move either of her arms." He added: "Both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what if any function she will regain in her arms."
In the later updates, given on Wednesday to the BBC, Ferrell said Pike was continuing to experience the after-effects of the drug pentobarbital.
The drug was injected into her body in two doses by prison staff during the scheduled execution on 30 September. But once it became clear that Pike was not going to die from the execution attempt, she was taken to hospital, where she was initially unconscious and declared to be in a critical condition.
As of late on Wednesday, though, Pike was "fairly well", Ferrell said.
"What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she's not able to use them very much."
Of her physical movements, Ferrell added: "She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far."
Turning to her mental state, he said: "I think it's kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she's also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she's going."
Ferrell said much remained unknown about what happens next. "I assume [the situation for Pike] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don't know that yet."
He added that the team wanted Pike to receive psychological support, since that "clearly is necessary now".
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her then-boyfriend
Ferrell and his colleagues - who highlighted ahead of the attempted execution that Pike had a condition that would make the injection method difficult - oppose any new attempt by state prison authorities to follow the same approach.
They are also calling on the state governor, Bill Lee, to downgrade Pike's punishment to the lesser sentence of life in prison without parole.
Meanwhile, Tennessee's proponents of capital punishment have suggested that a different method be used. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for state governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair."
Asked during a court hearing on Wednesday whether the state intended to reschedule Pike's execution, the state's attorney general said he did not know.
For now, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution.
Wednesday's court hearing related to the preservation of evidence following the first attempt.
The judge, I'Ashea Myles, ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels.
The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt.
She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.
Correction 8 October: This article originally said that Pike and her boyfriend had first met Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp for "troubled teens". This has been amended to make clear that the scheme was for low-income youths aged 16 to 24 and was not specifically for troubled teenagers.
Could the US death penalty ever die out? A surreal story about a man in Acton, London, who supplied the USA with lethal drugs tips Livvy Haydock into the macabre world of Death Row.

I interviewed Christa Pike 20 years ago - I can't stop thinking about her

title: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
summary: The German sportswear brand wants the Sydney-based label to stop selling the clothes and pay damages.
body:
Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo.
The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused.
The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile.
The Australian law firms representing Adidas and White Fox both declined to comment on the case, the first hearing due to begin on Friday.
In Federal Court documents, Adidas states that its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957.
The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark.
White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims.
It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items.
This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim.
The company says White Fox is "taking advantage" of Adidas's reputation, "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind".
Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs.
Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops.
In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes.
A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image.
In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes.
White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024.
In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review.

title: Mark Zuckerberg has an image problem - so why is Meta's business booming?
summary: A new film paints the Meta founder as a villain. But the tech firm seems immune to bad publicity, writes our North America tech correspondent.
body:
Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful.
"Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make."
Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists.
It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company.
For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users.
That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case.
And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him.
This year Meta unveiled Muse, its AI companion app, alongside a Tamagotchi-like wearable device that allows users to talk to it
His reputation is unlikely to be helped by The Social Reckoning, a film by Aaron Sorkin released this week. It's about whistleblower claims that Meta executives were aware of their products harming young people. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to a review in the Hollywood Reporter, "stoically arguing that even the slightest gesture of responsibility is anathema where money is concerned".
Some speculate that this is Meta's "Big Tobacco" moment, with a consensus forming against the company, and the social media industry as a whole.
But the truth seems to be more complicated. Despite months of bad press, in the real world Meta's products are doing better than ever. Use of its apps continues to rise, and users are already flocking to its new AI assistant.
It raises the question: can anything really clip Meta's wings? Or is it now something of a 'Teflon' company, with scandals simply bouncing off it?
It's certainly been a year of bad headlines for Meta.
Last summer, Reuters revealed that Meta allowed its chatbots to "engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual", and provide false medical information to users.
Meta has revised those policies and said that such responses should never have been allowed.
And this year, bills have been mounting. In March, a jury gave $6m (£4.5m) to a 20-year-old California woman who claimed she suffered mental health harms related to her use of Meta's Instagram and Google's YouTube.
Around the same time, New Mexico became the first state to succeed in a lawsuit against Meta over child safety issues. A jury found the company had failed to warn the public about the dangers its platforms posed to kids. Meta was fined a total of $942m. The judge called Meta a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution.
Meta says it disagrees with the verdicts and is appealing both cases.
Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to one review of The Social Reckoning
In May, Meta was among the social companies that avoided a trial by settling a case brought by a Kentucky school district that claimed their product design had led to a youth mental health crisis. Meta reportedly agreed to pay $9m, the most of any defendant.
And this summer, Meta struck a high-profile $18bn settlement with 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Meta denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement, and during the five-day trial it maintained that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for young users, pouring resources into testing and research. As part of the deal, the firm promised to enact two-hour daily time limits for young users, along with night-time blocks on use, muted notifications during school hours, and other changes.
The company faces other lawsuits too, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, also related to alleged social media addiction among young users.
Meanwhile, several countries have moved to ban social media for children entirely, starting with Australia last December. Social media companies are broadly disliked, even while their products remain wildly popular. A Reuters/Ipsos survey suggests that 85% of Americans think social media can be addictive for children, and 61% support greater government oversight.
Meta faces lawsuits over its handling of young social media users. Outside one case in California this summer, protesters highlighted the names of young people they say died as a result of social media harms. Meta disputes many of the claims
To some, the trust issue feels existential
"Once the public has stopped trusting you, it's kind of a downward spiral," says associate professor Alison Taylor of New York University's Stern School of Business.
"It feels like… the trust deficit is so big, I just don't know that they're going to be able to recover."
But despite those high-profile cases, the company reported that the number of people using some of its apps (like Instagram and WhatsApp) has risen 3% year on year and this year's second quarter revenue was up 28% compared with the same period in 2025.
While it has agreed to temper its pursuit of the teen market (which many brands eagerly cultivate to build their future user base), the company has said that teens accounted for less than 1% of its revenue anyway. Competitors TikTok and Google's YouTube are more popular with young users.
And the company's settlement with the 48 states was widely considered a massive win for Meta, because it prevented some Meta bosses (including Zuckerberg) from having to give testimony, and stopped the release of further internal documents, while allowing the company to avoid admitting wrongdoing. The company's stock price surged 4% immediately following the announcement, and is up more than 25% over the last month.
One view popular among critics is that the company has tested consumer tolerance for bad behaviour and until now, its business has mostly managed to withstand the blowback. In other words, people will continue to use the products even if they don't like the company.
"I think they're in a remarkably good position that I didn't expect them to be in," says Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy.
However, Meta's move into AI depends partly on rebuilding public trust.
Last month, the company launched its new AI personal assistant app, Muse. Crucially, Muse is an AI agent, meaning it can carry out tasks in multiple stages and work on something over several hours (in contrast to chatbots like ChatGPT, which tend to do one task at a time).
It's the first AI agent from a major tech firm to become publicly available. A New York Times tech reporter who used the app for two weeks says he was "blown away"; the app called his dental insurer on his behalf, ordered him groceries and tracked his credit card spending in a spreadsheet.
But Muse works best when users hand over some of their most personal information to the company, including credit card information, purchase histories and access to email inboxes.
It's a big ask for a company whose reputation on privacy has been sullied, starting a decade ago with the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which followed the revelation that the data of millions of Facebook users was breached and used by a political consulting firm.
Zuckerberg launched Facebook in 2004, aged 19, while studying at Harvard University
Just two days after Zuckerberg's keynote at Meta Connect, another New Mexico jury found Meta lied about how Facebook used personal information. (The company has said it disagrees with the verdict and will defend itself against what it says are efforts to distort its record.)
So are customers willing to hand over that data for the convenience of using Muse?
Some users say yes. Since its launch one month ago, Muse already has more than five million downloads and more than three million weekly active users - outpacing the adoption of ChatGPT when that was first introduced, in the North American market.
Zuckerberg has laid out a vision in which Muse couples with an ever-expanding line-up of Meta AI smart glasses, enabling users to summon hands-free what he calls "personal superintelligence".
Meta clearly has big plans for its smart glasses. "I think they're making an investment to position themselves as a category leader," says Kate Winick, principal analyst at Forrester, covering social media and influencers. "However big this category turns out to be, they will own it - for now."
Zuckerberg attended President Trump's inauguration ceremony last year, along with Elon Musk and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos
The glasses are divisive, and have been labelled by some as "pervert glasses" because they can be used to film covertly. The company has moved to stop users from tampering with the light that indicates a photo or video is being captured. Zuckerberg also just announced new audio-only smart glasses, an apparent bid to quell privacy concerns.
But the company's most strident critics remain wary.
"Consumers know that Meta has problems, and that to date we haven't been able to trust them to make their products safe for children. So why would a consumer want to trust them with some of their most private and sensitive information?" says Brooke Istook of the Heat Initiative, a campaign group.

title: 'Add me to WhatsApp' scam calls to be investigated
summary: The UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" that appear to lead to a recruitment scam.
body:
The UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" - where a recorded voice asks you to add them on WhatsApp - that are suspected to lead to a recruitment scam.
The Information Commission's Office (ICO) had more than 3,600 complaints about automated calls in September - a five-year high and nearly three times the number it had in July.
But it suspects millions of people are getting these calls and toldBBC Radio 4's You and Yoursit was "deeply concerned" by the sharp rise.
The ICO advises people to ignore calls from numbers they don't recognise, and to block and report any suspicious calls to the watchdog.
The automated calls typically come from what appears to be a UK mobile number.
Some of the recorded messages mention an offer of part-time work.
Simon Fell, from the Communications Crime Strategy Group, a telecoms industry body set up to tackle fraud, said he couldn't be sure exactly what form the scam would take as he hadn't followed up on the messages.
"Mostly likely it would be arecruitment scam," he said.
You and Yours added one of these numbers on WhatsApp and received this message
"They would either put you through to a fake job listing, which might involve some form of money muling. It could look like a completely legitimate job, or something ad hoc, but they might pass criminal funds through your account which can lead to terrible consequences.
"It could also be a simple phishing exercise - criminals send out these messages, and what they really want to know is who's picking up, who's active - that information can be resold on the dark web.
"The possibilities are endless. At the end of the day this is a criminal that has reached out to you and they're trying to defraud you in some way shape or form."
Andy Curry, the ICO's head of criminal investigations, told the BBC he believed the calls were coming from abroad.
"We are trying to find who is behind this, why they're doing it and the impact it's having on members of the public," he said.
The number of complaints received by the ICO would only be a small proportion of the totals affected, he said.
"We think there are probably millions of people who are receiving these messages, which appear to us to be largely indiscriminate.
"I've had them, my colleague who's leading the investigation has had them. It's likely to be tip of the iceberg."
'I lost my savings after a job interview scam'
Rise in reports of 'shameful' recruitment scams
Fell said that mobile companies were "working on a range of fronts" to tackle the influx of automated calls.
This includes sending intelligence reports to the regulator Ofcom, working with law enforcement, and liaising with Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because if someone does follow up on the request to add the number to the encrypted platform, "any dialogue that happens between you and the criminal then can't be investigated any further".
A WhatsApp spokesman said there were features in place to protect its users from scam calls, including silencing calls from unknown numbers. He also said WhatsApp banned millions of accounts each year for "malicious behaviours", such as bulk account registration or automated messaging.
While these calls typically appear to be from a UK mobile number, Fell said these numbers will be imitated, or spoofed, by the criminals behind the scam.
Last November, the UK governmentpromised,externalthat call spoofing would be eliminated within a year.
A Home Office spokesman said the government was taking "robust action" to tackle scams.
"We remain committed to delivering the Telecommunications Charter, alongside industry, by November," he added.

title: 'I don't know what my partner earns': How soon into dating should you reveal your salary?
summary: Talking about salary, spending habits and debt can be some of dating's trickier conversations.
body:
Watch: How soon into dating do you talk about your salary? We ask New Yorkers and Londoners
You know their favourite restaurant, what happened with their ex and their most embarrassing childhood story. But do you know how much your partner earns?
Money remains one of dating's trickier conversations. Bring it up too early and it can sound like you're sizing up their bank balance. But leave it too long and you could be planning a future with someone without knowing much about their finances at all.
We spoke to 20-somethings in New York City to see if there was a sweet spot for when to talk salaries.
Willa says she doesn't know what her partner earns even though he knows her salary
Willa Morton, 25, says she doesn't think couples necessarily need to reveal their salaries at all.
"It's just a number and you can gauge how much someone makes based on the way they live and how much they spend," she says.
Willa, who works in tech sales, has talked to her boyfriend about not earning very much herself but hasn't asked him for a figure in return.
He's a company founder and, though his income varies, she knows that he earns more than she does.
"He's more free-spending whereas I'm always saying, 'That's too expensive, that costs too much, we don't need to spend that.'"
Their dates typically cost around $200 (£150) and he usually pays, while she picks up smaller bills such as coffees.
"It's an unspoken rule that he will pick up the bigger bills."
Vik says if someone brought up salary and spending on a first date they probably wouldn't be the right person for him
For many, there's a fairly clear dividing line as to when you talk about salary, spending habits and debt and that's when you become an official couple.
Alexa Ludato, 25, who works in insurance, says she'd only have the conversation when she was official with someone.
Before then, she would "like to have an idea of what their job is, but not how much they make".
Her friend, Vik Sunderaj, 22, agrees. "You should only discuss it once you get into a serious relationship."
He thinks a salary question on the first few dates is "a little crazy".
"If they asked, I would be honest, but I wouldn't bring it up," he says. And if his date really wanted to know his salary, "it probably means they wouldn't be the right person for me".
Others feel even more strongly about being asked too soon. Twenty-six-year-old Bridget Shurdut, who works in sales, says she would find it "incredibly odd" if someone asked about her salary within the first few dates.
"I don't think I'd continue to see that person. I'd answer the question, but it would be a red flag for me."
For her, someone's current salary isn't necessarily particularly useful information anyway as she says she's much more interested in "whether someone is ambitious and driven than what they earn monetarily".
Dating and relationship coach Kate Mansfield, says money conversations "should start much earlier than many people think".
"In the first few dates you should talk about how each of you approaches spending, saving, generosity, lifestyle and financial independence as these things shape compatibility."
Emily's been in a relationship for two years and has not discussed salaries yet
Becoming official doesn't necessarily mean swapping payslips though.
Insurance worker Emily Moretta, 26, has been with her boyfriend for two years and says they still haven't explicitly told each other their salaries and "he doesn't know how much I make".
She assumes he probably has a rough idea, but says neither has ever felt the need to ask.
"Maybe down the line we would, when it gets more serious," she says, adding that they would have to be at the stage of moving in together before talking about it.

title: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring program
summary: An international visa program has for years allowed US tech companies to hire highly skilled workers from abroad.
body:
The White House has often made extreme claims regarding international workers and immigration.
Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program.
Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft alongside other firms of committing fraud through the use of the H1b visa programme and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents.
Vance claimed that Microsoft, one of the most valuable companies in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants."
Microsoft said most of the H1b visas filed over the last financial year were for existing workers, who are paid the same as local staff.
"No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
He also made similar accusations about Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.
The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said during the same conference.
Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers.
The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment.
The total number of H1b visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process,is capped,externalat 85,000 per year.
A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employs more than 200,000 people worldwide.
Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H1b visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace domestic workers and "undercut" their wages.
The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H1b visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires.
She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H1b visa program are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive.
According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, themedian salary,externalfor an H1b worker at Microsoft is $155,000.
"We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said.
Satya Nadella, Microsoft's long-time chief executive, was at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump.
Trump presented Nadella with a national medal of technology and innovation
Introducing Nadella during the event, Trump said the White House was "honoured" to be awarding the medal to him and that it was "so well-deserved".
Other tech industry figures to receive medals from Trump were Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Lisa Su, Sergey Brin, and Michael Dell.
Nadella and most of the other medal recipients were also present at other recent White House events, including a lunch on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping.
Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday.
"Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said.
He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US.
Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US governmentproposed eliminating,externalthat grace period altogether.
Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H1b visa program, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more.
None of those companies were included in Vance's Thursday comments.
The program has been aimed at highly skilled or specialized workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades.
The PERM program is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely.
During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Laborcertified,externalmore than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories.

title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
summary: Retailer issues update after BBC contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond "basic contact details"
body:
Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.
It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.
Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbersand dates of birth are now in the hands of criminals.
One victim told the BBC it was "very unsettling" that the hackers now know these things about her.
The criminals also have access to the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.
Harriet has been using Asos since 2019 - another detail the hackers now know.
"What I find particularly worrying is the possibility that stolen data can be used as a tool for for future attacks, meaning the impact of a breach could extend well beyond the initial incident," she said.
With the stolen information, scammers may be able to create convincing phishing attack emails or phone calls.
The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.
In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed.
"Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said.
"We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."
The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.
Customers saw this pop up notification on Tuesday
The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.
Later that day the firm confirmed to shareholders via the London Stock Exchange that the pop up was sent by an "unauthorised third party" and "basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed."
The company then sent an email to customers with similar wording.
On Wednesday evening the cyber criminals responsible contacted the BBC sharing a sample of the stolen data which showed the true extent of the hack.
The BBC held off publishing this article to allow Asos to contact its customers first.
Asos said it is still investigating the data breach and it would "contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required".
The UK fashion site explained to customers that hackers gained access to an Asos employee account by "impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials".
With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data.
In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance".
Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins.
The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data.
Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached.
Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action.
But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity.
"Passwords have not been stolen, so be highly suspicious of any unsolicited text or email asking you to change or share yours," said Trevor Dearing, Senior Director of Critical Infrastructure at Illumio.
"Expect scammers to mention the attack, use your personal details to seem genuine, and create urgency, such as threatening to lock your account within 24 hours."
Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information".
"We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said.

title: Polanski failed to show leadership over Zionism motion, ex-Green leader says
summary: Caroline Lucas tells the BBC Zack Polanski should have taken part in a vote on a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.
body:
Zack Polanski failed to show leadership over a motion passed by Green Party members declaring Zionism a form of racism, the party's former leader Caroline Lucas has told the BBC.
Lucas told Newsnight that the party's current leader, who did not attend the debate on the motion at the Green Party's annual conference in Brighton, "should have been there and he should have voted".
She described the motion, which defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state", as "dangerous" and "divisive".
In the wake of the vote, Polanski has said he will not accept anyone being excluded from the Green Party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of".
Lucas's comments came after polls closed in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where Polanski is standing as a candidate.
Polanski did not vote on the motion after leaving the party's conference early to campaign in the north London constituency.
The Green leader has declined media interviews since the motion was passed on Sunday and did not answer questions from a BBC reporter about the motion earlier on Thursday.
The motion also backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.
Lucas, who voted against the motion, said: "I would have hoped [Polanski] would have been a very strong critic of this motion."
She added that it was "flawed from top to bottom".
Asked if Polanski should stand down, she told Newsnight: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this by-election.
"I want him to speak now about what's happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday.
"I think the jury is out about whether he will do that - but I very much hope he will."
In response to Lucas's comments, a Green Party source said: "There are ups and downs in politics and when people are passionate they disagree in the heat of a campaign.
"We do things differently - unlike Labour who use anonymous sources and resort to  factionalism."
Watch: Polanski was asked earlier on Thursday about the Zionism conference motion
The motion has overshadowed the final days of Polanski's by-election campaign, where the Greens have been looking to overturn a substantial Labour majority in the seatvacated by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer.
It has sparkeddays of controversyand exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.
Four of the five Green MPs opposed the motion, while the party's co-deputy leaders were split over whether they supported it.
The vote also led to the resignation of the Green deputy leader in Wales and condemnation from the European Green Party.
In a written statement on Monday, Polanski did not specify whether he supported the motion passed by members but sought to reassure Jewish members that "no-one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith, or where they worship".
Polanski, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".
Ahead of the vote, he had backed an amendment to specify that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist, but this was voted down by members.
He had also said he wanted to see the reference to a single Palestinian state changed, arguing: "I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should be deciding what the future settlement looks like."
I won't accept exclusion within Green Party, says Polanski after criticism of Zionism motion
Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote
Polanski banned from Israel after party's motion declaring 'Zionism is racism'
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Polanski to reverse the motion and ensure it is not Green Party policy.
In his first comment on the row, Burnham said it was "completely wrong" for the party to support the motion and this showed "terrible judgement".
The PM said he felt the motion effectively ruled out a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine.
"For that reason, it shouldn't be supported in any way, shape or form," he told reporters while on a visit to Berlin.
When asked if he would rule out entering into coalition with the Greens, he would not be drawn on "any business about what might or might not happen in the future".
On Thursday, a Green Party spokesperson said: "This has been an emotive issue and is complex. It has rightly caused much discussion, and needs to be taken in the context that Israel's behaviour has had.
"Israel has been responsible for a genocide, ethnic cleansing and the killing of children, and we've had a political establishment which has not only turned a blind eye but provided support."
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is currently hearing a case brought by South Africa that accuses Israeli forces of genocide, but it could take years to reach a conclusion. Israel has called the case "wholly unfounded" and based on "biased and false claims".

title: UK and Germany will face threats together, says Burnham in Berlin
summary: Ahead of a UK-EU summit next month, Burnham said he was committed to "see if we can bring the UK closer to Europe".
body:
Andy Burnham is meeting Chancellor Friedrich Merz on his first official visit to Germany
The UK and Germany will face threats together, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said as he reaffirmed a series of defence and security partnerships.
On his first official European trip, apart from visits to Ukraine, Burnham met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and was greeted with military honours in Berlin.
Speaking to reporters at the German capital's Federal Chancellery, the prime minister said both countries were facing hybrid attacks "on a regular basis" and "it makes sense" to take them on together.
The pair formally ratified the2025 Kensington Treaty, a partnership committing both countries to tackle hostile activity.
Burnham said the treaty would "improve our security here in Europe" but also help grow the economy and living standards.
"The Kensington Treaty [is] the first treaty between Germany and the UK since the Second World War - it really is a significant moment," he said.
He added that the UK government would now "seek to progress" Germany joining Gcap, the Global Combat Air Programme led by Italy, Japan and the UK to develop a next-generation fighter aircraft.
He outlined partnerships "countering hybrid attacks" and "countering interference in our democratic processes".
He mentioned collaboration on quantum technology and space, adding he was aiming to host the first joint meeting of the UK and German cabinets next year.
The Berlin talks come after intelligence services warned of rising threats, including last month when Germany accused Russia oflaunching a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
The meeting was held at the Chancellery building in Berlin
Meanwhile, French finance minister Roland Lescure has invited Britain to"come all the way"back to the European Union, in an interview with the BBC's economics editor Faisal Islam.
Ahead of a UK-EU summit next month, Burnham said he was "very committed to securing deeper cooperation" and to "see if we can bring the UK closer to Europe".
He told reporters a closer relationship with Europe was in the interests of growth and tackling irregular migration.
In recent weeks he has mentioned the prospect of eventually rejoining the bloc.
The German leader replied: "From our German side, I can assure you that we will do anything what we can do to bring the UK closer and closer back to Europe, to the European continent, to the European Union."
'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UK
Plans for direct train to Berlin in new UK-Germany treaty
The meeting comes as European leaders have been warning that the threat of hybrid attacks against Europe by Russia has intensified.
Hybrid attacks can include potentially destabilising activity such as cyber attacks, sabotage or misinformation.
Sir Mark Lyall Grant, former UK national security adviser, explained that hybrid warfare "falls somewhere between peace and war - it's in that sort of grey zone, an area where Russia has been extremely active for some time".
He told Radio 4's Today that while Russia had posed a threat to the UK since Vladimir Putin became president in 2001, there had been an "intensification" in response to European support for Ukraine following Russia's invasion.
"We know Russia has been mapping undersea cables in the North Sea; that's something I'm sure Andy Burnham will be talking to Chancellor Merz about because it affects both the UK and Germany," he added.
Last month, a senior Russian diplomat was summoned by the British government over an "egregious and reckless attack" on Leipzig airport, while the EU's foreign affairs chief also summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels.
Burnham was greeted with German military honours
It is a major international freight hub used for providing support to Ukraine. Moscow has denied any involvement in the incident.
Meanwhile, questions have been raised this week about Germany's reliability as an intelligence partner, following the bombshell arrest of a formerspy chief on suspicion of espionage.
The talks also come during a period in which Merz's own political future has come under intense scrutiny.
Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, after the former leader was forced out by his own MPs just two years after winning a landslide election victory.
Similarly, Merz has faced persistent rumours he could be replaced by his party due to his poor approval ratings and followingsetbacks in regional elections.
Although the chancellor appears to have overcome an immediate crisis in his leadership, questions remain over his future.

title: Clubs fear political interference in Man City appeal
summary: Premier League clubs are "concerned" about political interference in Manchester City's appeal after Prime Minister Andy Burnham's comments.
body:
Andy Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 until he became prime minister this summer
Some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by comments made by Andy Burnham - appearing to downplay the verdict againstManchester City- that they are now "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process, sources have told BBC Sport.
Senior club figures say they were shocked when they heard the prime minister tell the BBC he would be"really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell upafter the club werefound guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.
They have questioned what his comments to the BBC were designed to achieve, and said it had put the Independent Football Regulator in a difficult position.
Burnham is under increasing pressure surrounding his relationship with the club's Abu Dhabi ownership during his time as mayor of Greater Manchester.
Such is the level of scrutiny that Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.
Asked to respond to the BBC's story on Thursday, Burnham said: "No I haven't downplayed the seriousness of the findings. They are findings that need to be considered with great care and seriousness and then the process that considers them needs to be fully independent.
"I said that last week and I will repeat it again. I think it's incumbent on everybody now to let the process run its course.
"I was asked a question about wider investment. I think it's important to separate the football issues from wider investment. The football issues have to be looked at fully and that is without question."
Despite clarification from Downing Street that Burnham's view is that no-one is "above the rules", his comments sparked unease among some senior Labour figures who fear his initial comments have had major cut-through with voters.
